As the interests and career opportunities for our students have become more diverse, we are seeking to allow more flexibility in selecting professional electives most appropriate for each individual.
The best preparation for many students is something in between our existing Pre-Professional Exercise Science and Applied Exercise Science specializations.
Additionally, it is currently difficult for students who begin in the Pre-Professional Exercise Science specialization and then realize it is not the best fit to change to the Applied Exercise Science specialization without impeding progress toward graduation.
This proposal combines the Professional Content Area courses from each of those specializations into a single list of Professional Electives students can select from.
It will replace the existing Pre-Professional and Applied Exercise Science specialization options in the catalog, but in practice will allow students to choose Professional Electives aligning with either of those specializations or a combination of the two.

The Kinesiology program is currently accredited by the Committee on Accreditation for the Exercise Sciences and this proposal will not change anything associated with that accreditation.
This specialization continues to provide opportunities for students to participate in the department's active research program and community engagement opportunities through active learning courses and internships in alignment with the University's Mission.
It provides the basic science and core kinesiology content area background as well as professional elective options necessary to prepare students for careers that have a great impact on social, cultural, and economic ecosystems in RI and beyond (Strategic Plan Goal 1) including many in healthcare.
The specialization allows students opportunities for study abroad and international internship experiences such as the TEAN program placing our majors in internships in Australia (Strategic Plan Goal 2 Action 3).
Students will also be able to gain hands on research experience working with faculty throughout the department (Strategic Plan Goal 3).

The only specializations this overlaps with are our department's current specializations of Pre-Professional Exercise Science and Applied Exercise Science.
This proposal will replace both of those with this single Kinesiology specialization, so there will be no lasting conflicts or overlaps.
Students currently in the Pre-Professional Exercise Science and Applied Exercise Science specializations will be able to complete the programs they have already started, and incoming students will be entered into the new Kinesiology specialization.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-2 January 23, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting Context (from JCODL 2022-2023 final report): “Several years ago (circa 2013), URI adopted definitions of online and blended learning (Face to face [< 25% online], Blended [25-75% online], and Online [75-100% online]), with the implicit, but unstated, assumption that the online portion was asynchronous.
The COVID era of remote instruction gave rise to additional approaches to remote instruction and the need to reflect all available modality options and to provide clear, comprehensible and accessible definitions and descriptions for the benefit of faculty and students.” Rationale: The “adopted” definitions are not memorialized in the University Manual and the current need to update modality-related descriptions provides an opportunity to provide standardized language in the University Manual, where it will be easily found and understood.
The language is proposed for insertion into Chapter 8, Academic Regulations (Regulations for Students), Section 30, Courses.

Existing modalities will translate into new modalities as follows: 1. ‘In-person’ � ‘In-person’ 2. ‘Blended’ � ‘In-person and online asynchronous’ or ‘In-person and online synchronous’ 3. ‘Online’ � ‘Online synchronous’ or ‘Online synchronous and asynchronous’ or ‘Online asynchronous’.
Because current ‘online’ and ‘blended’ modality courses will need to be assigned to a new modality (perhaps more than one if multiple faculty teach the same course using different modalities), faculty/departments will be allowed to update the modality of current ‘online’ and ‘blended’ modality courses directly with the registrar without going through the standard course modification process.
A course change proposal will not be necessary if faculty/departments teaching a class in one of the three ‘in-person’ modalities (‘In-person’, ‘In-person and online asynchronous’, ‘In-person and online synchronous’) wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) another of the ‘in-person’ modalities.

A course change proposal will not be necessary if faculty/departments teaching a class in one of the three ‘online’ modalities (‘Online synchronous’, ‘Online synchronous and asynchronous’, ‘Online asynchronous’) wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) another of the ‘online’ modalities.
As per current practice, course change proposals will continue to be necessary for courses with one of the three ‘in-person’ modalities that wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) one of the three ‘online’ modalities.
This is also true for ‘online’ modality courses that wish to adopt/add an ‘in-person’ modality.
Because of the volume of required changes, the new modalities will take effect starting in the Fall 2026 semester.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-03 Faculty Senate Meeting of January 23, 2025 Resolution on the Implementation of Honors Contracts WHEREAS, following considerable self-study and significant input from external experts, the URI Honors Program has proposed the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements, facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They allow students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS, contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership by enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences”; and WHEREAS, honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS, honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when student/faculty constraints or funding limitations preclude offering stand-alone honors courses that fit student interests and needs; and WHEREAS, Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for the self-guided intellectual growth of students; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.
This includes making the

recommended changes to the University Catalog and to the eCampus system used by Enrollment Services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Honors Program is called upon to reflect these changes on their website and in all other promotional and outreach materials promulgated by the Program. The Program is also called upon to review Chapter 8 of the University Manual (Academic Regulations, Honors Program) in light of the Contracts Proposal and bring any recommended changes to the Faculty Senate expeditiously; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the authority to offer Honors Contracts enabled by this resolution shall not extend beyond the Fall 2025 semester; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that no instructor may participate in more than three Honors Contracts in a single semester. Adopted this 23rd day of January, 2025. ____________________________________________________________ T heodore Walls, URI Faculty Senate President

The competition among MSM programs is intense, with a large number of institutions offering these degrees.
Programs strive to differentiate themselves by emphasizing unique curricular components such as leadership development modules, capstone projects, or global immersion experiences, which are designed to enhance employability and prepare graduates for management roles.
The rise of digital learning technologies has also led many institutions to offer MSM programs in online or hybrid formats, further increasing their reach and intensifying competition as geographic barriers to enrollment are reduced.
To stand out in a crowded market, programs often seek accreditation from prestigious bodies like AACSB, AMBA, or EQUIS and aim to secure favorable rankings from notable publications.
Many programs also forge partnerships with businesses and other organizations to help in curriculum development, provide real-world learning opportunities, and facilitate networking and job placements for graduates.

Recent trends in MSM programs include an increased emphasis on technology and analytics to integrate digital technologies in business, a focus on sustainability and social responsibility reflecting broader societal concerns, and more customizable and flexible learning paths to attract a diverse student body with varying needs and career goals.
Overall, the market for MSM programs remains robust, driven by their relevance, accessibility, and adaptability to market needs and educational technologies, though programs must continuously innovate and adapt to remain competitive.

V. 23.09.29 CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE FACULTY SENATE OFFICE URI Curriculum & Standards Committee Non-Standard form for curricular changes Only to be used in cases not appropriate for Kuali A Proposal to Fully Integrate the Public Relations Program into the Department of Journalism, Creating a New Department of Journalism and Public Relations Date: 10/27/23 Proposer Name: Professor Norbert Mundorf Department: Communication Studies 1.
Describe the change you are proposing.
This organization change will bring the Public Relations B.A. program, which is currently housed in the Communication Studies department, and the Journalism B.A. program together in a new Journalism and Public Relations department. 2.
Give the rationale for your proposed change.
In 1997, the B.A. in Public Relations was approved as an interdepartmental program jointly run by the Communication Studies department and the Journalism department.

The original legislation (Bill #96- 97-26) called for the program to be administered on a “three-year rotating basis by the Chairs of Journalism and Communication Studies” with an “advisory/admissions committee” comprised of both chairs from the respective departments and the faculty who taught in the program.
Somewhere in the twenty-five plus years that have elapsed since the original proposal, the Public Relations program was effectively subsumed by Communication Studies and the interdepartmental structure of the original vision was lost.
During the academic program review of Journalism this past year, external reviewers suggested the Journalism curriculum would benefit from a “rethinking of [Harrington’s] overall department structure.” While it was originally proposed that the department might merge with the program in Sports Media Communication, subsequent conversations with faculty suggested that public relations would be a better fit as this pairing is common in institutions across the country and presents additional opportunities for collaboration due to the curricular overlap between the two programs.
